intro:
Bilingual restaurant staff and phone orders work best when the phone process is simple, not improvised. The goal is to get the order right, make the caller feel comfortable, and keep the line moving.

If your team speaks more than one language, that is a strength. If not, you can still handle bilingual callers well with a clear script, a few translated phrases, and a backup plan like [call forwarding codes by carrier](/tools/call-forwarding-codes) or an AI phone host such as ROAL.

sections.h2: Why bilingual phone coverage matters on busy shifts
sections.body:
Phone orders can stack up fast during lunch, dinner, and weekends. If the person answering does not share the caller’s language, the call can take longer, the order can come through wrong, or the caller may hang up and try somewhere else.

That is especially common for pizza shops, delis, and takeout spots where people want quick answers. A simple phone script helps even when only one person on the team speaks Spanish, or when the bilingual staff member is in the kitchen.

Use this opening line:
- "Gracias por llamar. One moment, please."
- "Thank you for calling. How can I help you?"

Short checklist for the shift:
1. Decide who handles the phone first.
2. Keep the menu, prices, and specials near the phone.
3. Write down the most common item names in both languages.
4. Make sure someone can step in for allergy or manager calls.

If you want a bigger-picture staffing angle, see [turnover and keeping phone know-how](/blog/restaurant-employee-turnover).

sections.h2: What should bilingual staff say on the phone?
sections.body:
The best script is short and repeatable. Staff should not translate every menu detail from memory. They should collect the same facts every time: item, size, modifiers, notes, name, phone number, and ready time.

A practical script for a bilingual caller:
1. Greeting: "Hola, gracias por llamar. What can I get for you?"
2. Order: "Is that large or medium?" or "¿Grande o mediana?"
3. Details: "Any extra cheese, onions, or no onions?"
4. Confirmation: "So that is two chicken tacos, one large cheese pizza, pickup at 6:20."

A few useful phrases to keep on a note card:
| English | Spanish |
|---|---|
| pickup | para recoger |
| delivery | entrega |
| ready time | tiempo de recogida |
| name | nombre |
| phone number | número de teléfono |
| extra sauce | salsa extra |

This is not about perfect translation. It is about making the order clear enough to send to the kitchen without a callback.

sections.h2: How do I train bilingual phone coverage without slowing the kitchen?
sections.body:
Training should focus on speed and consistency. A caller should hear the same basic flow no matter who answers. That keeps the dining room, prep line, and phone from pulling in different directions.

Try this 4-step training plan:
1. Pick one standard greeting for the whole team.
2. Practice the top 20 items in both languages.
3. Teach staff when to stop and get help.
4. Review one or two live calls each week.

Example with numbers you can swap for your own:
- Say your average phone order is $28.
- If a call takes 2 extra minutes because staff are translating on the fly, that can slow the next call and the ticket flow.
- If a bilingual script cuts that confusion, you keep the line moving and the kitchen gets cleaner tickets.

sections.h2: When should a bilingual call go to staff instead of staying on the phone?
sections.body:
Not every call should stay with the phone host or the first staff member who answers. Some calls need a person, especially when the customer has a complaint, a food allergy question, a catering request, or a manager request.

A good handoff rule is simple:
- Keep the call on the phone for standard pickup and delivery orders.
- Escalate if the caller asks about allergens, large catering, missing food, refunds, or special handling.
- Pass along a short summary so staff do not have to start from zero.

Example handoff script:
- "One moment while I get the manager."
- "I’m sending this to the kitchen with your notes."

You can also keep a written escalation list near the register:
| Call type | Who handles it |
|---|---|
| Standard order | phone staff or phone host |
| Sold-out item question | staff or phone host with menu notes |
| Allergy question | manager or trained staff |
| Catering order | manager |
| Complaint | manager |

For owner-level decisions, see [what calls should reach the manager](/blog/restaurant-manager-phone-escalations).

sections.h2: How can I support bilingual callers when my team is short-staffed?
sections.body:
Short-staffed shifts are where bilingual coverage gets hardest. The phone keeps ringing while the line is moving, someone is packing bags, and the only bilingual team member may be doing something else.

A backup plan helps:
1. Route the main number to a reliable line during rushes.
2. Keep a short bilingual greeting ready.
3. Use one person to confirm orders before they go out.
4. Move unusual calls to a manager or inbox instead of guessing.

If you use call forwarding, confirm the exact code with your carrier and test it with a real call. On many landlines and some carriers, *72 forwards all calls and *73 turns it off. On some GSM mobile carriers, **21*number# forwards all calls and ##21# turns it off, while **61*number# may forward unanswered calls and **67*number# may forward busy calls. Verizon Wireless commonly uses *72, *73, and *71 for busy/no-answer forwarding. Business VoIP systems usually handle forwarding in the web portal.

For owners who want a cleaner fallback, ROAL can answer the phone, speak the caller’s language, and hand the tough calls to staff with a summary. That keeps bilingual coverage from depending on one person being in the right place at the right moment.

sections.h2: What is the simplest setup for bilingual phone orders?
sections.body:
The simplest setup is one that matches how your restaurant already works. You do not need a full overhaul. You need a clear menu source, a phone path, and a way to confirm orders before they hit the kitchen.

A practical setup looks like this:
- Use your website, menu PDF, or menu photos as the source of truth.
- Keep hours and address current.
- Make sure sold-out items are marked so they are not offered.
- Decide which calls should go to staff.
- Keep the phone number you already use and forward it when needed.

sections.h2: How do I measure whether bilingual phone coverage is working?
sections.body:
Do not measure this by gut feeling alone. Look at simple things your staff already sees every day: how often orders need callbacks, how many calls turn into clean tickets, and whether the kitchen has to fix avoidable mistakes.

Try this owner worksheet for one week:
| Metric | Your number |
|---|---|
| Calls answered on first try | ___ |
| Orders taken without a callback | ___ |
| Calls sent to staff for special help | ___ |
| Orders that reached the kitchen screen cleanly | ___ |
| Common phrase staff kept repeating | ___ |

If you pay a bilingual staff member to sit at the phone during busy hours, plug in your own wage rate and hours worked. If you compare that to other options, keep the math honest. Delivery apps commonly take roughly 15-30% commission per order, human answering services usually bill per minute or per call, and many monthly AI phone tools charge a fixed fee whether or not orders come in. ROAL uses pay-per-completed-order pricing, with no monthly fee, no setup fee, and no per-minute fee.

takeaways: A short bilingual script is better than improvising every call.
Standard orders can stay on the phone; allergy, complaint, and catering calls should go to staff.
Test your forwarding setup with a real call and confirm carrier codes before relying on them.

faq.q: How do bilingual restaurant staff handle phone orders fast?
faq.a: Use one short script for every call: greet, take the order, confirm items and modifiers, collect the name and phone number, and repeat the order back. Keep the menu and common phrases within reach so staff do not have to guess. The goal is clear information, not perfect translation.

faq.q: What should I do if my staff only speaks one language?
faq.a: Use a simple fallback plan. Forward the phone during busy times, keep a translated cheat sheet for the most common items, and send tricky calls to a manager or inbox. An AI phone host can also handle standard orders and language switching, while staff handle the calls that need judgment.
